name: Lincoln-Douglas Debate
aka: LD, Value Debate, Lincoln-Douglas Value Debate
summary: One debater against one on a question of values: what is just, right or good, and what standard should decide it.
who: High school students (and some middle school divisions) debating one on one. The NSDA, state associations, and the homeschool leagues NCFCA and Stoa all offer it.
resolution: A value resolution that changes during the season. NSDA members vote on topics, which run for two months at a time (the national tournament has its own).
named: Named for the 1858 Illinois Senate campaign debates between Abraham Lincoln and Stephen Douglas, which were about the morality and politics of slavery's spread.

speeches.name: Affirmative Constructive
speeches.speaker: Aff
speeches.job: Present the value, the criterion, definitions and the contentions for the affirmative.

speeches.name: Negative Constructive
speeches.speaker: Neg
speeches.job: Present the negative case and refute the affirmative case.

speeches.name: First Affirmative Rebuttal
speeches.speaker: Aff
speeches.job: Refute the negative case and rebuild the affirmative case, in four minutes against seven.

speeches.name: Negative Rebuttal
speeches.speaker: Neg
speeches.job: Refute the affirmative, rebuild the negative, and give voting issues.

speeches.name: Second Affirmative Rebuttal
speeches.speaker: Aff
speeches.job: Answer the negative's voting issues and give the affirmative's.

prep.note: Four minutes for each debater during the round (NSDA, Stoa). NCFCA allows three, and not right before cross-examination.

rewards: Clear thinking about values and how to weigh them
Philosophy put in plain words a judge can follow
Time management, especially in the affirmative's short rebuttals
start: Read the current topic and list the values at stake on each side.
Learn the value and criterion structure in the Framework chapter.
Write a six-minute affirmative case and a seven-minute negative case with two contentions each.
Practice the 1AR: answer a seven-minute speech in four minutes.
Watch the final round of a national tournament on video and flow it.
varies: Prep time: four minutes (NSDA, Stoa) or three minutes (NCFCA); some local tournaments set their own.
Topics: NSDA topics run two months; NCFCA and Stoa choose their own resolutions for the year.
Style: some national-circuit rounds are fast and technical; most local, state and homeschool rounds expect a clear, persuasive pace for a lay judge.
Whether a value and criterion are required: traditional and homeschool LD expect them; some circuits accept other frameworks.

p: Each side names a **value** (the goal the round should be judged by, such as justice or human dignity) and a **criterion** (how to measure whether that value is met). Then each side shows, with contentions, that its side of the resolution best meets the standard.
The affirmative speaks first and last. The time split is uneven on purpose: the affirmative gets 13 minutes of speaking and the negative 13, but the negative's rebuttal comes in one six-minute block.
